1 | # Waypoint — Adaptive Codebase Onboarding
     2 | 
     3 | Waypoint turns Python, JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Java, HTML, and CSS repositories into an
     4 | evidence-aware code graph and a role-specific onboarding workspace. It uses
     5 | static analysis only: analyzed repository code is never imported or executed.
     6 | 
     7 | ## Architecture
     8 | 
     9 | ```mermaid
    10 | flowchart TD
    11 |     UI[React + TypeScript UI] -->|HTTP /api/v1| API[FastAPI application]
    12 |     API --> IMPORT[Local path or secured GitHub clone]
    13 |     IMPORT --> ANALYZER[Python AST + Tree-sitter analyzers]
    14 |     ANALYZER --> GRAPH[Typed code graph]
    15 |     ANALYZER --> INDEX[Revision-aware SQLite index]
    16 |     INDEX --> SEARCH[FTS5/BM25 + local vectors]
    17 |     GRAPH --> SEARCH
    18 |     API --> MEMORY[SQLite conversations and sessions]
    19 |     API --> AGENT[Repository agent runner]
    20 |     AGENT --> INVESTIGATE[Investigation model]
    21 |     INVESTIGATE --> TOOLS[Bounded repository tools]
    22 |     TOOLS --> SEARCH
    23 |     TOOLS --> GRAPH
    24 |     AGENT --> SYNTHESIZE[Synthesis model]
    25 |     SYNTHESIZE --> VALIDATE[Pydantic tool + answer + citation validation]
    26 |     VALIDATE --> UI
    27 |     UI --> COMPARE[Independent two-agent comparison]
    28 |     COMPARE --> TOOLS
    29 |     MCP[MCP server: 30 tools] --> GRAPH
    30 |     MCP --> SEARCH
    31 |     HOOKS[Pre / post / error hooks and JSONL traces] -.observe.-> API
    32 |     HOOKS -.observe.-> AGENT
    33 |     HOOKS -.observe.-> TOOLS
    34 | ```
    35 | 
    36 | FastAPI and Pydantic provide typed HTTP boundaries and generated OpenAPI; React,
    37 | TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React Flow, and Monaco provide the interactive evidence
    38 | workspace. SQLite keeps the project locally deployable while persisting graph sessions,
    39 | chunks, lexical/vector indexes, issues, and conversation memory. The model layer supports
    40 | OpenRouter, the Anthropic API, and the Claude Agent SDK. In dual mode a low-cost model can
    41 | investigate through tools while a stronger model synthesizes a validated answer.
    42 | 
    43 | The detailed verification package, including coverage, Flask HTTP E2E, live multi-step
    44 | agent evidence, and same-question two-model comparison, is in
    45 | [`verification/README.md`](verification/README.md). Significant AI-assisted engineering
    46 | interactions are recorded in [`prompts.md`](prompts.md).
    47 | 
    48 | ## What is included

    50 | - Python AST extraction for modules, classes, functions, methods, imports, and calls
    51 | - Tree-sitter extraction for JavaScript/JSX, TypeScript/TSX, Java, HTML, and CSS
    52 | - ES module imports/re-exports, CommonJS `require`, Java packages/imports, lexical
    53 |   containment, and conservatively inferred calls
    54 | - Explicit class-instantiation edges plus locally constructed receiver resolution for
    55 |   cross-file Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Java method calls
    56 | - Exact source spans, confidence, and unresolved-reference diagnostics
    57 | - Scalable React Flow visualization with on-demand neighborhood expansion
    58 | - Read-only Monaco source viewer and evidence inspector
    59 | - Claude-powered repository Q&A with bounded retrieval tools and validated citations
    60 | - revision-aware SQLite code indexing with persisted chunks, symbols, edges, file
    61 |   hashes, FTS5/BM25 search, and automatic refresh when repository contents change
    62 | - local subword-vector retrieval, reciprocal-rank fusion, graph expansion, index
    63 |   status/rebuild controls, and restart-safe issue/onboarding state
    64 | - pre/post/error function hooks, correlated model/tool/retrieval traces, rotating JSONL
    65 |   diagnostics, and a 30-tool MCP connector over stdio or Streamable HTTP
    66 | - readable GitHub-flavored Markdown rendering …<1000 chars truncated>

1 | # External repository benchmarks
     2 | 
     3 | This suite validates the analyzer against shallow clones of established Python
     4 | repositories. Clones live outside the application workspace by default at
     5 | `C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks`.
     6 | 
     7 | The benchmark verifies:
     8 | 
     9 | - Parse success and performance
    10 | - Unique, stable node and edge identities
    11 | - Valid graph endpoints
    12 | - Valid source spans
    13 | - Evidence-status invariants
    14 | - Correct package names for flat and `src/` layouts
    15 | - Known architectural modules, classes, methods, and functions
    16 | - First-party import resolution
    17 | 
    18 | Run:
    19 | 
    20 | ```powershell
    21 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_repositories.py `
    22 |   --fixtures-root C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks `
    23 |   --output benchmarks\results
    24 | ```
    25 | 
    26 | Use `--repository flask` to run one fixture. Results are written as JSON and
    27 | Markdown so changes in analyzer quality can be reviewed rather than inferred
    28 | from node counts alone.
    29 | 
    30 | ## Retrieval benchmark
    31 | 
    32 | The local retrieval benchmark measures file Hit@5, Hit@10, mean reciprocal rank,
    33 | nDCG@10, indexing/restoration time, cold/warm query latency, latency percentiles, and
    34 | process peak memory against known evidence files:
    35 | 
    36 | ```powershell
    37 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval.py `
    38 |   --repository . `
    39 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-latest.json
    40 | ```
    41 | 
    42 | Add repository-specific cases by supplying another JSON file with `--cases`.
    43 | 
    44 | V3 also contains a 50-question, three-repository development benchmark with explicit
    45 | development/held-out labels, required path groups, forbidden distractors, repository and
    46 | language slices, and an adjudication gate. Pending seed labels are rejected unless the
    47 | caller explicitly opts into a non-release diagnostic:
    48 | 
    49 | ```powershell
    50 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval_v3.py `
    51 |   --repository waypoint=. `
    52 |   --repository flask=.waypoint-clones/pallets--flask--214023150b `
    53 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones/haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `
    54 |   --allow-unadjudicated `
    55 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-v3.json
    56 | ```
    57 | 
    58 | See `BENCHMARKS_AND_TESTS_V3.md` for formulas, limitations, and the preserved V2-to-V3
    59 | comparison.
    60 | 
    61 | ## V4 independent-agent benchmark
    62 | 
    63 | V4 uses a separate 50-case, four-repository corpus. Each fixed endpoint independently
    64 | chooses production repository tools; candidate results, explicit source reads, and final
    65 | citations are scored separately. The benchmark also records schema corrections, retries,
    66 | tokens, latency, and trace-correlated hook/log quality.

    72 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones\haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `

   257 |         name = node.qualified_name.lower()

   261 |         centrality = min(self.degree[node.id], 30) * 0.8
   262 |         support_code_penalty = (

   273 |                     "example",
   274 |                     "script",
   275 |                 )
   276 |             )

   278 |         )
   279 |         package_depth_penalty = max(0, name.count(".") - 3) * 0.5
   280 |         return (

   283 |             + support_code_penalty

   430 |     """Read-only query layer over one AnalysisReport's nodes/edges (neighborhoods, summaries, overviews).
   431 | 
   432 |     Wraps a single AnalysisReport with id-indexed node lookups so callers don't
   433 |     need to re-scan the full node/edge lists for every query. Instantiated
   434 |     per-request in backend/app/api/routes.py and backend/app/agent/retrieval.py
   435 |     (e.g. `GraphQueryService(session.report)`) to answer graph API/tool calls
   436 |     without mutating or persisting anything.
   437 |     """
   438 | 
   439 |     def __init__(self, report: AnalysisReport) -> None:
   440 |         """Indexes a report's nodes by id for fast lookup and keeps its edge list for traversal."""
   441 |         self.report = report
   442 |         self.nodes = {node.id: node for node in report.nodes}
   443 |         self.edges = report.edges
   444 | 
   445 |     @traced("graph.query.neighborhood")
   446 |     def neighborhood(self, node_id: str, depth: int) -> GraphNeighborhood:
   447 |         """Breadth-first-searches the undirected graph out to `depth` hops from `node_id` and returns that induced subgraph.
   448 | 
   449 |         Input: a `node_id` that must exist in `self.nodes` (raises `KeyError`
   450 |         otherwise) and a non-negative `depth`. Builds an undirected adjacency
   451 |         map from all edges, then BFS-expands the visited set hop by hop, and
   452 |         returns every node reached plus every edge whose both endpoints were
   453 |         reached. Called by backend/app/api/routes.py's neighborhood endpoint and
   454 |         backend/app/agent/retrieval.py wherever the agent needs a bounded local
   455 |         view around a specific node instead of the entire (possibly huge) graph.
   456 |         """
   457 |         if node_id not in self.nodes:
   458 |             raise KeyError(node_id)
   459 |         adjacency: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
   460 |         for edge in self.edges:
   461 |             adjacency.setdefault(edge.source, set()).add(edge.target)
   462 |             adjacency.setdefault(edge.target, set()).add(edge.source)
   463 |         visited = {node_id}
   464 |         queue: deque[tuple[str, int]] = deque([(node_id, 0)])
   465 |         while queue:
   466 |             current, current_depth = queue.popleft()
   467 |             if current_depth >= depth:
   468 |                 continue
   469 |             for neighbor in adjacency.get(current, set()):
   470 |                 if neighbor not in visited:
   471 |                     visited.add(neighbor)
   472 |                     queue.append((neighbor, current_depth + 1))
   473 |         selected_edges = [
   474 |             edge
   475 |             for edge in self.edges
   476 |             if edge.source in visited and edge.target in visited
   477 |         ]
   478 |         return GraphNeighborhood(
   479 |             center_node_id=node_id,
   480 |             depth=depth,
   481 |             nodes=[self.nodes[item] for item in visited],
   482 |             edges=selected_edges,
   483 |         )

class SemanticRepositoryTools:
    """Bounded deterministic architecture queries over one analyzed repository.

    Wraps an ``AnalysisSession`` graph report plus its ``RepositoryRetrievalIndex``
    to answer higher-level architecture questions (overview, entry points, layers,
    file structure, dependency impact, ...) as plain dict payloads with bounded
    source evidence, all backed by a per-revision result cache. Instantiated by
    backend/app/agent/service.py:RepositoryAgentService.__init__ (as ``self.semantic``)
    and by backend/app/mcp_server.py:_semantic for MCP tool handlers; its public
    methods are also exposed as agent tools (get_repository_overview,
    find_entry_points, etc.) so the LLM agent and the MCP surface share one
    implementation of these deterministic, non-LLM repository queries.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        session: AnalysisSession,
        index: RepositoryRetrievalIndex,
    ) -> None:
        """Indexes graph nodes/edges once and builds the outgoing/incoming edge and degree lookups.

        Input: `session` is the AnalysisSession for one analyzed repository revision;
        `index` is the RepositoryRetrievalIndex used to read source text and to share
        the semantic result cache. Called wherever a SemanticRepositoryTools instance
        is created (RepositoryAgentService.__init__, backend/app/mcp_server.py:_semantic,
        and tests); precomputing adjacency/degree here avoids re-scanning the full
        edge list on every subsequent query method call.
        """
        self.session = session
        self

def search(self, revision_id: str, query: str, limit: int) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
        """Run a SQLite FTS5 full-text query for one revision, ranked by bm25.

        Input: revision_id; query - raw query string (tokenized here into
        identifier-like words, OR-ed together in the MATCH expression); limit -
        capped to 1-200. Uses `bm25(code_chunks_fts, 0, 0, 2.5, 4.0, 1.5, 1.0)`,
        weighting the `path` and `qualified_name` columns above raw `content` so
        filename/symbol-name hits outrank incidental content matches; bm25's rank
        is negated so higher scores are better here. Called by
        RepositoryRetrievalIndex.search as the lexical half of its hybrid ranking.
        """
        tokens = list(dict.fromkeys(_TOKEN.findall(query.lower())))
        if not tokens:
            return []
        expression = " OR ".join(f'"{token}"' for token in tokens)
        with self._lock, closing(self._connect()) as connection:
            self._initialize(connection)
            rows = connection.execute(
                "SELECT chunk_id, bm25(code_chunks_fts, 0, 0, 2.5, 4.0, 1.5, 1.0) AS rank "
                "FROM code_chunks_fts WHERE code_chunks_fts MATCH ? AND revision_id = ? "
                "ORDER BY rank LIMIT ?",
                (expression, revision_id, max(1, min(limit, 200))),
            ).fetchall()
            return [(str(row["chunk_id"]), -float(row["rank"])) for row in rows]

def _add_definition(
        self,

        kind: NodeKind,

        """Creates a GraphNode for a class/function/method AST node and links it to its lexical parent with a CONTAINS edge.

        Input: the definition `node` (ClassDef/FunctionDef/AsyncFunctionDef),

def _evidence(self, request: ModelComparisonRequest) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        """Search the repository index once for evidence matching the comparison question,
        so both models are handed the exact same frozen evidence.

        Input: request.question (str) and request.evidence_limit (int, max passages).

        evidence = self.index.search(
            request.question,

def score_paths(paths: list[str], labels: RetrievalLabels) -> RetrievalStageMetrics:
    """Score one ranked retrieval stage against explicit, versioned human labels."""
    ranked = _dedupe(paths)
    normalized = [_canonical(path) for path in ranked]
    groups = [
        {_canonical(path) for path in group if path}
        for group in labels.required_path_groups if group

    acceptable = {_canonical(path) for path in labels.acceptable_paths if path}
    relevant = acceptable | set().union(*groups) if groups else acceptable
    forbidden = {_canonical(path) for path in labels.forbidden_paths if path}

    def relevant_at(k: int) -> list[int]:
        return [1 if path in relevant else 0 for path in normalized[:k]]

    hits5 = relevant_at(5)
    hits10 = relevant_at(10)
    first_rank = next((index for index, hit in enumerate(relevant_at(len(ranked)), 1) if hit), None)

    group_hits = sum(bool(group.intersection(normalized)) for group in groups)
    dcg = sum(hit / math.log2(index + 2) for index, hit in enumerate(hits10))

    idcg = sum(1 / math.log2(index + 2) for index in range(ideal_hits))

def search_repository(
    analysis_id: str,
    query: str,
    limit: int = 12,
    path_prefixes: list[str] | None = None,
    symbol_kinds: list[str] | None = None,
    languages: list[str] | None = None,

    """Hybrid-search indexed source with optional path/language/symbol filters."""
    index = repository_indexes.get(_session(analysis_id))
    results = index.search(

        kinds=symbol_kinds,

    )
    return {"revision_id": index.revision_id, "count": len(results), "results": results}

def evaluate(repository: Path, cases_path: Path, repeats: int = 3) -> dict[str, object]:
    root = repository.resolve()
    cases = json.loads(cases_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    report = RepositoryAnalyzer().analyze(root).model_copy(
        update={"analysis_id": "retrieval-benchmark"}

    snapshot = repository_snapshot(root)

# Why a Rare Symbol Query and a Broad Architecture Question Produce Different Evidence Rankings

Waypoint's retrieval pipeline is implemented in `backend/app/agent/retrieval.py` as `RepositoryRetrievalIndex.search`. Every query passes through the same six stages, but the *inputs* to each stage differ dramatically between a rare symbol name (e.g. `_contextual_text`) and a broad architecture question (e.g. "how does the agent layer work?"). That difference cascades through every stage and produces a completely different ranked list.

---

## Stage 1 — Lexical Tokenisation & Stopword Removal

```python
_TOKEN = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{1,}")
_QUERY_STOPWORDS = {
    "about", "after", "also", "and", "are", "become", "can", "does",
    "explain", "for", "from", "give", "how", "into", "its", "main", "of",
    "our", "the", "their", "then", "through", "to", "used", "what", "when",
    "where", "which", "why", "with",
}
```

The query is lowercased and split into identifier-like tokens (≥ 2 chars, letter/underscore-led). Common English words are then stripped as stopwords.

- **Rare symbol query** (`_contextual_text`): after tokenisation you get `["contextual", "text"]` — two highly specific, low-frequency tokens. Almost nothing in the corpus contains both.
- **Broad architecture question** (`"how does the agent layer work?"`): after stopword removal you get `["agent", "layer", "work"]` — three common tokens that appear in dozens of files.

The token set is what drives every downstream stage, so the divergence starts here.

---

## Stage 2 — Lexical FTS5/BM25 Scoring

```python
expression = " OR ".join(f'"{token}"' for token in tokens)
rows = connection.execute(
    "SELECT chunk_id, bm25(code_chunks_fts, 0, 0, 2.5, 4.0, 1.5, 1.0) AS rank "
    "FROM code_chunks_fts WHERE code_chunks_fts MATCH ? AND revision_id = ? "
    "ORDER BY rank LIMIT ?",
    (expression, revision_id, max(1, min(limit, 200))),
).fetchall()
```

The FTS5 virtual table has four weighted columns: `path` (weight 2.5), `qualified_name` (weight 4.0), `contextual_text` (weight 1.5), and `content` (weight 1.0). BM25 rewards *rare* tokens more than common ones.

- **Rare symbol query**: `contextual_text` appears in very few chunks, and it appears in the `qualified_name` column (weight 4.0) for the exact method. BM25 assigns a very high IDF (inverse document frequency) to a rare token, so the one or two matching chunks receive an enormous score. The ranking is essentially deterministic — the exact symbol chunk wins by a large margin.
- **Broad architecture question**: `agent`, `layer`, and `work` are common words. BM25 IDF is low for all three. Many chunks match at least one token, so the score differences are small and the ranking is noisy. No single chunk dominates.

---

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

Waypoint does not copy a local repository into the database. Source is read from the

# Graph nodes and vector validity

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

1. Parser-derived graph nodes and typed edges.
2. Symbol-aware source chunks.
3. SQLite FTS5/BM25 lexical retrieval.
4. Deterministic local subword-vector retrieval.
5. Exact path, qualified-name, symbol-kind, and test-aware ranking signals.
6. Bounded graph-neighbor expansion around strong retrieved symbols.

## What are the graph nodes?

`backend/app/graph/models.py:9-15` defines five node kinds:

| Node | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `repository` | The analyzed repository as the graph root. |
| `module` | An analyzed source file/module. |
| `class` | A parser-discovered class or interface-like type. |
| `function` | A module-level or nested function. |
| `method` | A callable owned by a class. |

Nodes carry a stable ID, kind, short name, qualified name, module, source span,
signature, and metadata. They are static source-code entities, not runtime objects.
A runtime-like construction such as `UserService()` is represented as an
`instantiates` edge to the class node rather than a separate object-instance node.

The typed edges are:

- `contains`: repository/module/class lexical ownership;
- `imports`: one internal module imports another;
- `may_call`: a st

Pydantic validates the final answer schema. Invalid citations or fields are returned as
errors for another bounded attempt. An unvalidated answer never reaches the evidence
panel.

## 9. Answer presentation and memory

Only files cited in the validated final answer populate the Answer Evidence panel.
Conversation turns are persisted by analysis and scope, with only the configured recent
window sent back to the model. Symbol-inspector Ask preloads exact incoming/outgoing
usage evidence for the selected symbol.

## What the architecture is and is not

It is:

- agentic RAG;
- hybrid lexical/vector/graph retrieval;
- revision-aware and evidence-validating;
- local SQLite-first storage;
- static analysis with explicit uncertainty.

It is not currently:

- a dedicated graph database;
- an external vector database;
- a learned semantic-embedding system;
- runtime tracing of an analyzed application;
- proof that every `may_call` edge executed;
- full-repository dumping into every prompt.

# Waypoint Benchmark Methodology and Failure Analysis

## Release rule

The 70% threshold is a declared Waypoint release policy, not an industry-standard formula.
A run passes only when:

1. all required artifacts exist;
2. the equal-weight average of the five categories is at least 70%; and
3. every individual category passes its own 70% gate.

For model quality, every provider/model endpoint must additionally achieve at least 70%
task success. This is why the 83.16% model composite still fails: OpenRouter task success
was 50%.

The overall calculation was:

```text
(100.00 + 58.76 + 83.16 + 66.67 + 50.78) / 5 = 71.87%
```

The overall average clears 70%, but four category pass flags are false.

## Category formulas and pass criteria

### Parsing accuracy

```text
score = mean(parse success rate, node F1, relationship F1)
      = mean(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)
      = 100%
```

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

# Graph nodes and vector validity

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

1. Parser-derived graph nodes and typed edges.
2. Symbol-aware source chunks.
3. SQLite FTS5/BM25 lexical retrieval.
4. Deterministic local subword-vector retrieval.
5. Exact path, qualified-name, symbol-kind, and test-aware ranking signals.
6. Bounded graph-neighbor expansion around strong retrieved symbols.

## What are the graph nodes?

`backend/app/graph/models.py:9-15` defines five node kinds:

| Node | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `repository` | The analyzed repository as the graph root. |
| `module` | An analyzed source file/module. |
| `class` | A parser-discovered class or interface-like type. |
| `function` | A module-level or nested function. |
| `method` | A callable owned by a class. |

Nodes carry a stable ID, kind, short name, qualified name, module, source span,
signature, and metadata. They are static source-code entities, not runtime objects.
A runtime-like construction such as `UserService()` is represented as an
`instantiates` edge to the class node rather than a separate object-instance node.

The typed edges are:

- `contains`: repository/module/class lexical ownership;
- `imports`: one internal module imports another;
- `may_call`: a st

Pydantic validates the final answer schema. Invalid citations or fields are returned as
errors for another bounded attempt. An unvalidated answer never reaches the evidence
panel.

## 9. Answer presentation and memory

Only files cited in the validated final answer populate the Answer Evidence panel.
Conversation turns are persisted by analysis and scope, with only the configured recent
window sent back to the model. Symbol-inspector Ask preloads exact incoming/outgoing
usage evidence for the selected symbol.

## What the architecture is and is not

It is:

- agentic RAG;
- hybrid lexical/vector/graph retrieval;
- revision-aware and evidence-validating;
- local SQLite-first storage;
- static analysis with explicit uncertainty.

It is not currently:

- a dedicated graph database;
- an external vector database;
- a learned semantic-embedding system;
- runtime tracing of an analyzed application;
- proof that every `may_call` edge executed;
- full-repository dumping into every prompt.

# Waypoint Benchmark Methodology and Failure Analysis

## Release rule

The 70% threshold is a declared Waypoint release policy, not an industry-standard formula.
A run passes only when:

1. all required artifacts exist;
2. the equal-weight average of the five categories is at least 70%; and
3. every individual category passes its own 70% gate.

For model quality, every provider/model endpoint must additionally achieve at least 70%

This document describes the target storage and retrieval architecture for Waypoint. The
goal is to improve retrieval accuracy, latency, restart behavior, and observability
without introducing infrastructure that the current product does not yet need.

## Recommendation

```text

Language parser and graph analyzer

                    |

              Final reranking
                    |
                    v
          Bounded source evidence
                    |
                    v

                    |

          Citation-span validation
```

This keeps the existing agent and graph advantages while replacing the temporary
custom search index with a durable retrieval layer.

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

1. Parser-derived graph nodes and typed edges.
2. Symbol-aware source chunks.
3. SQLite FTS5/BM25 lexical retrieval.
4. Deterministic local subword-vector retrieval.
5. Exact path, qualified-name, symbol-kind, and test-aware ranking signals.
6. Bounded graph-neighbor expansion around strong retrieved symbols.

| `function` | A module-level or nested function. |
| `method` | A callable owned by a class. |

Similarity is a candidate-generation signal, not relationship evidence.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,

added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

1. Parser-derived graph nodes and typed edges.
2. Symbol-aware source chunks.
3. SQLite FTS5/BM25 lexical retrieval.
4. Deterministic local subword-vector retrieval.
5. Exact path, qualified-name, symbol-kind, and test-aware ranking signals.
6. Bounded graph-neighbor expansion around strong retrieved symbols.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## 1. Repository acquisition and security boundary

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public
HTTPS GitHub URL. GitHub repositories are shallow-cloned into the managed clone root
with credential prompting disabled, timeout/file/byte limits, symlink avoidance, and
retention cleanup.

The analyzer never treats an arbitrary requested path as the allowed root. It resolves
the requested repository and verifies containment under the separately configured root.

## 2. Multi-language static analysis

Waypoint discovers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX/TSX, and Java source while
skipping dependencies, VCS metadata, build output, caches, managed clones, symlinks, and
oversized files.

Python uses the standard AST. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java use Tree-sitter. Analysis
creates repository, module, class, function, and method nodes plus contains/imports/
may-call/instantiates edges. Every resolved edge carries source evidence and confidence;
failures remain explicit unresolved references.

External imports are classified separately and feed the synthetic External packages UI
card rather than being turned into fake internal graph nodes.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

# Waypoint RAG architecture

## 1. Repository acquisition and security boundary

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public
HTTPS GitHub URL. GitHub repositories are shallow-cloned into the managed clone root
with credential prompting disabled, timeout/file/byte limits, symlink avoidance, and
retention cleanup.

The analyzer never treats an arbitrary requested path as the allowed root. It resolves
the requested repository and verifies containment under the separately configured root.

## 2. Multi-language static analysis

Waypoint discovers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX/TSX, and Java source while
skipping dependencies, VCS metadata, build output, caches, managed clones, symlinks, and
oversized files.

Python uses the standard AST. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java use Tree-sitter. Analysis
creates repository, module, class, function, and method nodes plus contains/imports/
may-call/instantiates edges. Every resolved edge carries source evidence and confidence;
failures remain explicit unresolved references.

External imports are classified separately and feed the synthetic External packages UI
card rather than being turned into fake internal graph nodes.

`repository_snapshot()` walks retrievable files deterministically and stores, per file:

- normalized relative path;
- SHA-256 content hash;

# Current Database, Storage, and Retrieval Architecture

This document describes what Waypoint stores today, what exists only in memory, and
how a repository question reaches the language model. It reflects the current code,
not the intended future architecture.

## Executive summary

Waypoint currently uses a mixed persistence model:

- SQLite persists analysis reports, recent conversations, revisioned code chunks,
  normalized symbols and edges, file hashes, and an FTS5 search index.
- The analyzed repository remains the authoritative source for file contents.
- Parsed graph nodes and edges are serialized as one JSON analysis report in SQLite.
- Retrieval chunks are persisted per immutable content revision and also cached in
  memory while active.
- AI issue findings and onboarding challenge/mastery state persist in SQLite.
- There is an FTS5/BM25 index and a local deterministic subword-vector index, but no
  external vector database, learned embedding provider, or dedicated graph database.

The existing question-answering path is already a form of agentic, graph-augmented
RAG. Claude chooses bounded retrieval tools, receives source evidence, and writes an
answer whose citations must refer to inspected spans. The weak point is not the
agent loop. The current index provides durable lexical and local subword-vector
retrieval; learned semantic embeddings and incremental reuse of unchanged records
remain future work.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

# Waypoint RAG architecture

## 1. Repository acquisition and security boundary

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public
HTTPS GitHub URL. GitHub repositories are shallow-cloned into the managed clone root
with credential prompting disabled, timeout/file/byte limits, symlink avoidance, and
retention cleanup.

The analyzer never treats an arbitrary requested path as the allowed root. It resolves
the requested repository and verifies containment under the separately configured root.

## 2. Multi-language static analysis

Waypoint discovers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX/TSX, and Java source while
skipping dependencies, VCS metadata, build output, caches, managed clones, symlinks, and
oversized files.

Python uses the standard AST. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java use Tree-sitter. Analysis
creates repository, module, class, function, and method nodes plus contains/imports/

failures remain explicit unresolved references.

External imports are classified separately and feed the synthetic External packages UI
card rather than being turned into fake internal graph nodes.

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

1. Parser-derived graph nodes and typed edges.
2. Symbol-aware source chunks.
3. SQLite FTS5/BM25 lexical retrieval.
4. Deterministic local subword-vector retrieval.
5. Exact path, qualified-name, symbol-kind, and test-aware ranking signals.
6. Bounded graph-neighbor expansion around strong retrieved symbols.

## What are the graph nodes?

`backend/app/graph/models.py:9-15` defines five node kinds:

| Node | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `repository` | The analyzed repository as the graph root. |
| `module` | An analyzed source file/module. |
| `class` | A parser-discovered class or interface-like type. |
| `function` | A module-level or nested function. |
| `method` | A callable owned by a class. |

Nodes carry a stable ID, kind, short name, qualified name, module, source span,
signature, and metadata. They are static source-code entities, not runtime objects.
A runtime-like construction such as `UserService()` is represented as an
`instantiates` edge to the class node rather than a separate object-instance node.

The typed edges are:

- `contains`: repository/module/class lexical ownership;
- `imports`: one internal module imports another;

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## 1. Executive summary

Waypoint is a graph-assisted, retrieval-augmented repository agent. It does not send an entire repository to an LLM. The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

The evidence channels are:

2. Symbol-aware source chunks.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## Production retrieval changes

### 1. Query stopword removal

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,

# Waypoint RAG architecture

## 1. Repository acquisition and security boundary

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public
HTTPS GitHub URL. GitHub repositories are shallow-cloned into the managed clone root
with credential prompting disabled, timeout/file/byte limits, symlink avoidance, and
retention cleanup.

The analyzer never treats an arbitrary requested path as the allowed root. It resolves
the requested repository and verifies containment under the separately configured root.

## 2. Multi-language static analysis

Waypoint discovers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX/TSX, and Java source while
skipping dependencies, VCS metadata, build output, caches, managed clones, symlinks, and
oversized files.

Python uses the standard AST. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java use Tree-sitter. Analysis
creates repository, module, class, function, and method nodes plus contains/imports/
may-call/instantiates edges. Every resolved edge carries source evidence and confidence;
failures remain explicit unresolved references.

External imports are classified separately and feed the synthetic External packages UI
card rather than being turned into fake internal graph nodes.

## 3. Immutable repository revision

`repository_snapshot()` walks retrievable files deterministically and stores, per file:

- normalized relative path;
- SHA-256 content hash;
- byte size.

The aggregate path/content digest is the repository fingerprint. Repository ID,
fingerprint, and index schema version produce an immutable revision ID. A content change
therefore produce

# Prompting fundamentals expressed in Waypoint

## 1. Explicit role and objective

Each workflow receives a narrow role rather than one universal vague prompt:

- evidence-first repository analyst;
- adaptive onboarding planner;
- safe first-contribution planner;
- credible issue investigator;
- evidence-rubric assessor.

The user question, onboarding role, objective, experience, and time budget are included
as runtime context instead of being replaced by predetermined answer templates.

## 2. Tool-oriented decomposition

The prompt tells the model to investigate before answering and explains when specialized
tools are preferable: overview/feature tools for repository summaries, entry-point tools
for startup, architecture tools for layers, and symbol/test/impact tools for focused
questions. Tool schemas constrain names, argument types, limits, and required fields.

This is agentic tool prompting rather than “put the entire repository in one prompt.”

## 3. Evidence grounding and epistemic discipline

The prompts distinguish:

- documentation evidence for product claims;
- implementation source for behavioral claims;
- verified syntax from static inference;
- possible calls from proven runtime behavior;
- proposed issues from maintainer-confirmed issues.

The model is instructed not to invent files, symbols, behavior, line numbers, or issues.
The backend then enforces inspected-range citations independently, so grounding is more
than a verbal instruction.

## 4. Prompt-injection boundary

Repository content is explicitly declared untrusted data. Prompts say never to follow

High-frequency question words such as `how`, `where`, `what`, `and`, `through`, and `with` are removed from lexical scoring. Raw terms are retained separately for intent detection. Previously, a large unrelated file could receive a high score simply because it repeated common prose words.

### 2. Conservative morphology expansion

The retriever adds singular and conservative `-ed`/`-ing` variants. For example, `conversations` can match `conversation`, and `stored` can match `store`. This improves matches between natural-language questions and identifier/source vocabulary without introducing a model dependency.

### 3. Capped term frequency

Each informative term contributes at most three raw occurrences per chunk. This stops long files from winning solely through repetition.

### 4. Distinct-concept coverage

Scoring now rewards the fraction of distinct query concepts represented by a chunk. A chunk matching several parts of the question outranks one repeating a single term many times.

### 5. Stronger path relevance

## Why SQLite before a graph database

Waypoint already has graph semantics, but its expected queries are bounded one- or
two-hop traversals inside one repository. Indexed edge tables handle those efficiently
while also allowing analysis, conversations, FTS, and product state to share one
transactional local database.

A dedicated graph database would add deployment, synchronization, authentication,
backup, and migration complexity without fixing the first-stage retrieval problem.
The immediate problem is locating the correct seed symbols for a question; BM25 and
semantic retrieval improve that directly.

Adopt a dedicated graph database only when measurements show requirements such as:

- Millions of symbols and relationships in a routinely queried graph.
- Frequent deep, variable-length multi-hop queries.
- Cross-repository or organization-wide dependency analysis.
- High concurrent graph query and update volume.
- Latency demonstrably dominated by indexed SQL edge traversal.

## Is Waypoint agentic RAG over graph nodes?

Waypoint is agentic hybrid RAG over several evidence channels, not graph nodes alone.
The model can choose repository-search, bounded source-reading, symbol, graph, semantic,
test, configuration, and diagnostic tools over multiple rounds. Retrieved results are
added to its conversation before it synthesizes an answer.

# Waypoint RAG architecture

## 1. Repository acquisition and security boundary

The user selects a local repository under `ONBOARD_ALLOWED_ROOT` or supplies a public
HTTPS GitHub URL. GitHub repositories are shallow-cloned into the managed clone root
with credential prompting disabled, timeout/file/byte limits, symlink avoidance, and
retention cleanup.

The analyzer never treats an arbitrary requested path as the allowed root. It resolves
the requested repository and verifies containment under the separately configured root.

## 2. Multi-language static analysis

Waypoint discovers Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, JSX/TSX, and Java source while
skipping dependencies, VCS metadata, build output, caches, managed clones, symlinks, and
oversized files.

Python uses the standard AST. JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java use Tree-sitter. Analysis
creates repository, module, class, function, and method nodes plus contains/imports/
may-call/instantiates edges. Every resolved edge carries source evidence and confidence;
failures remain explicit unresolved references.

External imports are classified separately and feed the synthetic External packages UI
card rather than being turned into fake internal graph nodes.

## 3. Immutable repository revision

`repository_snapshot()` walks retrievable files deterministically and stores, per file:

- normalized relative path;
- SHA-256 content hash;
- byte size.

The aggregate path/content digest is the repository fingerprint. Repository ID,
fingerprint, and index schema version produce an immutable revision ID. A content change
therefore produce

# Prompting fundamentals expressed in Waypoint

## 1. Explicit role and objective

Each workflow receives a narrow role rather than one universal vague prompt:

- evidence-first repository analyst;
- adaptive onboarding planner;
- safe first-contribution planner;
- credible issue investigator;
- evidence-rubric assessor.

The user question, onboarding role, objective, experience, and time budget are included
as runtime context instead of being replaced by predetermined answer templates.

## 2. Tool-oriented decomposition

The prompt tells the model to investigate before answering and explains when specialized
tools are preferable: overview/feature tools for repository summaries, entry-point tools
for startup, architecture tools for layers, and symbol/test/impact tools for focused
questions. Tool schemas constrain names, argument types, limits, and required fields.

This is agentic tool prompting rather than “put the entire repository in one prompt.”

## 3. Evidence grounding and epistemic discipline

The prompts distinguish:

- documentation evidence for product claims;
- implementation source for behavioral claims;
- verified syntax from static inference;
- possible calls from proven runtime behavior;
- proposed issues from maintainer-confirmed issues.

The model is instructed not to invent files, symbols, behavior, line numbers, or issues.
The backend then enforces inspected-range citations independently, so grounding is more
than a verbal instruction.

## 4. Prompt-injection boundary

Repository content is explicitly declared untrusted data. Prompts say never to follow

1 | # External repository benchmarks
     2 | 
     3 | This suite validates the analyzer against shallow clones of established Python
     4 | repositories. Clones live outside the application workspace by default at
     5 | `C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks`.
     6 | 
     7 | The benchmark verifies:
     8 | 
     9 | - Parse success and performance
    10 | - Unique, stable node and edge identities
    11 | - Valid graph endpoints
    12 | - Valid source spans
    13 | - Evidence-status invariants
    14 | - Correct package names for flat and `src/` layouts
    15 | - Known architectural modules, classes, methods, and functions
    16 | - First-party import resolution
    17 | 
    18 | Run:
    19 | 
    20 | ```powershell
    21 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_repositories.py `
    22 |   --fixtures-root C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks `
    23 |   --output benchmarks\results
    24 | ```
    25 | 
    26 | Use `--repository flask` to run one fixture. Results are written as JSON and
    27 | Markdown so changes in analyzer quality can be reviewed rather than inferred
    28 | from node counts alone.
    29 | 
    30 | ## Retrieval benchmark
    31 | 
    32 | The local retrieval benchmark measures file Hit@5, Hit@10, mean reciprocal rank,
    33 | nDCG@10, indexing/restoration time, cold/warm query latency, latency percentiles, and
    34 | process peak memory against known evidence files:
    35 | 
    36 | ```powershell
    37 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval.py `
    38 |   --repository . `
    39 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-latest.json
    40 | ```
    41 | 
    42 | Add repository-specific cases by supplying another JSON file with `--cases`.
    43 | 
    44 | V3 also contains a 50-question, three-repository development benchmark with explicit
    45 | development/held-out labels, required path groups, forbidden distractors, repository and
    46 | language slices, and an adjudication gate. Pending seed labels are rejected unless the
    47 | caller explicitly opts into a non-release diagnostic:
    48 | 
    49 | ```powershell
    50 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval_v3.py `
    51 |   --repository waypoint=. `
    52 |   --repository flask=.waypoint-clones/pallets--flask--214023150b `
    53 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones/haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `
    54 |   --allow-unadjudicated `
    55 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-v3.json
    56 | ```
    57 | 
    58 | See `BENCHMARKS_AND_TESTS_V3.md` for formulas, limitations, and the preserved V2-to-V3
    59 | comparison.
    60 | 
    61 | ## V4 independent-agent benchmark
    62 | 
    63 | V4 uses a separate 50-case, four-repository corpus. Each fixed endpoint independently
    64 | chooses production repository tools; candidate results, explicit source reads, and final
    65 | citations are scored separately. The benchmark also records schema corrections, retries,
    66 | tokens, latency, and trace-correlated hook/log quality.
    67 | 
    68 | ```powershell
    69 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_agentic_retrieval_v4.py `
    70 |   --repository waypoint=. `
    71 |   --repository flask=.waypoint-clones\pallets--flask--214023150b `
    72 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones\haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `
    73 |   --repository open-notebook=.waypoint-clones\lfnovo--open-notebook--5d0a28a4b0 `
    74 |   --endpoint openrouter:poolside/laguna-m.1:free `
    75 |   --endpoint openrouter:poolside/laguna-xs-2.1:free `
    76 |   --max-cases 50 `
    77 |   --allow-unadjudicated `

    48 |     anything about the model's hidden reasoning process.

1 | # Waypoint — Adaptive Codebase Onboarding
     2 | 
     3 | Waypoint turns Python, JavaScript, TypeScript/TSX, Java, HTML, and CSS repositories into an
     4 | evidence-aware code graph and a role-specific onboarding workspace. It uses
     5 | static analysis only: analyzed repository code is never imported or executed.
     6 | 
     7 | ## Architecture
     8 | 
     9 | ```mermaid
    10 | flowchart TD
    11 |     UI[React + TypeScript UI] -->|HTTP /api/v1| API[FastAPI application]
    12 |     API --> IMPORT[Local path or secured GitHub clone]
    13 |     IMPORT --> ANALYZER[Python AST + Tree-sitter analyzers]
    14 |     ANALYZER --> GRAPH[Typed code graph]
    15 |     ANALYZER --> INDEX[Revision-aware SQLite index]
    16 |     INDEX --> SEARCH[FTS5/BM25 + local vectors]
    17 |     GRAPH --> SEARCH
    18 |     API --> MEMORY[SQLite conversations and sessions]
    19 |     API --> AGENT[Repository agent runner]
    20 |     AGENT --> INVESTIGATE[Investigation model]
    21 |     INVESTIGATE --> TOOLS[Bounded repository tools]
    22 |     TOOLS --> SEARCH
    23 |     TOOLS --> GRAPH
    24 |     AGENT --> SYNTHESIZE[Synthesis model]
    25 |     SYNTHESIZE --> VALIDATE[Pydantic tool + answer + citation validation]
    26 |     VALIDATE --> UI
    27 |     UI --> COMPARE[Independent two-agent comparison]
    28 |     COMPARE --> TOOLS
    29 |     MCP[MCP server: 30 tools] --> GRAPH
    30 |     MCP --> SEARCH
    31 |     HOOKS[Pre / post / error hooks and JSONL traces] -.observe.-> API
    32 |     HOOKS -.observe.-> AGENT
    33 |     HOOKS -.observe.-> TOOLS
    34 | ```
    35 | 
    36 | FastAPI and Pydantic provide typed HTTP boundaries and generated OpenAPI; React,
    37 | TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React Flow, and Monaco provide the interactive evidence
    38 | workspace. SQLite keeps the project locally deployable while persisting graph sessions,
    39 | chunks, lexical/vector indexes, issues, and conversation memory. The model layer supports
    40 | OpenRouter, the Anthropic API, and the Claude Agent SDK. In dual mode a low-cost model can
    41 | investigate through tools while a stronger model synthesizes a validated answer.
    42 | 
    43 | The detailed verification package, including coverage, Flask HTTP E2E, live multi-step
    44 | agent evidence, and same-question two-model comparison, is in
    45 | [`verification/README.md`](verification/README.md). Significant AI-assisted engineering
    46 | interactions are recorded in [`prompts.md`](prompts.md).
    47 |

1 | # External repository benchmarks
     2 | 
     3 | This suite validates the analyzer against shallow clones of established Python
     4 | repositories. Clones live outside the application workspace by default at
     5 | `C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks`.
     6 | 
     7 | The benchmark verifies:
     8 | 
     9 | - Parse success and performance
    10 | - Unique, stable node and edge identities
    11 | - Valid graph endpoints
    12 | - Valid source spans
    13 | - Evidence-status invariants
    14 | - Correct package names for flat and `src/` layouts
    15 | - Known architectural modules, classes, methods, and functions
    16 | - First-party import resolution
    17 | 
    18 | Run:
    19 | 
    20 | ```powershell
    21 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_repositories.py `
    22 |   --fixtures-root C:\tmp\waypoint-benchmarks `
    23 |   --output benchmarks\results
    24 | ```
    25 | 
    26 | Use `--repository flask` to run one fixture. Results are written as JSON and
    27 | Markdown so changes in analyzer quality can be reviewed rather than inferred
    28 | from node counts alone.
    29 | 
    30 | ## Retrieval benchmark
    31 | 
    32 | The local retrieval benchmark measures file Hit@5, Hit@10, mean reciprocal rank,
    33 | nDCG@10, indexing/restoration time, cold/warm query latency, latency percentiles, and
    34 | process peak memory against known evidence files:
    35 | 
    36 | ```powershell
    37 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval.py `
    38 |   --repository . `
    39 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-latest.json
    40 | ```
    41 | 
    42 | Add repository-specific cases by supplying another JSON file with `--cases`.
    43 | 
    44 | V3 also contains a 50-question, three-repository development benchmark with explicit
    45 | development/held-out labels, required path groups, forbidden distractors, repository and
    46 | language slices, and an adjudication gate. Pending seed labels are rejected unless the
    47 | caller explicitly opts into a non-release diagnostic:
    48 | 
    49 | ```powershell
    50 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_retrieval_v3.py `
    51 |   --repository waypoint=. `
    52 |   --repository flask=.waypoint-clones/pallets--flask--214023150b `
    53 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones/haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `
    54 |   --allow-unadjudicated `
    55 |   --output benchmarks\results\retrieval-v3.json
    56 | ```
    57 | 
    58 | See `BENCHMARKS_AND_TESTS_V3.md` for formulas, limitations, and the preserved V2-to-V3
    59 | comparison.
    60 | 
    61 | ## V4 independent-agent benchmark
    62 | 
    63 | V4 uses a separate 50-case, four-repository corpus. Each fixed endpoint independently
    64 | chooses production repository tools; candidate results, explicit source reads, and final
    65 | citations are scored separately. The benchmark also records schema corrections, retries,
    66 | tokens, latency, and trace-correlated hook/log quality.
    67 | 
    68 | ```powershell
    69 | .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe benchmarks\run_agentic_retrieval_v4.py `
    70 |   --repository waypoint=. `
    71 |   --repository flask=.waypoint-clones\pallets--flask--214023150b `
    72 |   --repository praw=.waypoint-clones\haxtheweb--praw--69db9269ab `
    73 |   --repository open-notebook=.waypoint-clones\lfnovo--open-notebook--5d0a28a4b0 `

244 | def _agent_error(exc: Exception) -> HTTPException:
   245 |     """Converts an agent-layer exception into the matching HTTPException.
   246 | 
   247 |     Input: any Exception raised by an AI-agent call, typically AgentUnavailableError
   248 |     or AgentExecutionError from backend/app/agent/service.py. Maps
   249 |     AgentUnavailableError (no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY configured) to 503, and everything
   250 |     else to 502 with the exception text as detail. Called by every route that
   251 |     invokes an LLM-backed agent (create_tour, answer_challenge, get_mission,
   252 |     answer_repository_question, compare_repository_answers, investigate_issues) so
   253 |     all AI-powered endpoints fail with a consistent status/response shape.
   254 |     """
   255 |     if isinstance(exc, AgentUnavailableError):
   256 |         return HTTPException(
   257 |             status_code=503,
   258 |             detail="ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is required for AI-generated repository answers",
   259 |         )
   260 |     return HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=str(exc))

   237 |     def __init__(self, report: AnalysisReport) -> None:
   238 |         self.report = report
   239 |         self.nodes = {node.id: node for node in report.nodes}
   240 |         self.edges = report.edges
   241 |         self.modules = [
   242 |             node for node in report.nodes if node.kind == NodeKind.MODULE
   243 |         ]
   244 |         self.degree = Counter[str]()
   245 |         self.outgoing = Counter[str]()
   246 |         self.incoming = Counter[str]()
   247 |         self.children = Counter[str]()
   248 |         for edge in self.edges:
   249 |             self.degree[edge.source] += 1
   250 |             self.degree[edge.target] += 1
   251 |             self.outgoing[edge.source] += 1
   252 |             self.incoming[edge.target] += 1
   253 |             if edge.kind == EdgeKind.CONTAINS:
   254 |                 self.children[edge.source] += 1
   255 | 
   256 |     def _role_score(self, node: GraphNode, role: DeveloperRole) -> float:
   257 |         name = node.qualified_name.lower()
   258 |         keyword_score = sum(
   259 |             16 for keyword in ROLE_KEYWORDS[role] if keyword in name
   260 |         )
   261 |         centrality = min(self.degree[node.id], 30) * 0.8
   262 |         support_code_penalty = (
   263 |             -35
   264 |             if role != DeveloperRole.QA
   265 |             and any(
   266 |                 part in name
   267 |                 for part in (
   268 |                     "test",
   269 |                     "fixture",
   270 |                     "conftest",
   271 |                     "benchmark",
   272 |                     "docs",
   273 |                     "example",
   274 |                     "script",
   275 |                 )
   276 |             )
   277 |             else 0
   278 |         )
   279 |         package_depth_penalty = max(0, name.count(".") - 3) * 0.5
   280 |         return (
   281 |             keyword_score
   282 |             + centrality
   283 |             + support_code_penalty
   284 |             - package_depth_penalty
   285 |         )
   286 | 
   287 |     @traced("tour.plan")
   288 |     def plan_tour(self, request: TourRequest) -> TourPlan:
   289 |         if not self.modules:
   290 |             raise ValueError("The analysis contains no source modules to tour")
   291 |         desired_steps = max(4, min(10, request.minutes // 3 + 2))
   292 |         ranked = sorted(
   293 |             self.modules,
   294 |             key=lambda node: (
   295 |                 -self._role_score(node, request.role),
   296 |                 node.qualified_name,
   297 |             ),
   298 |         )
   299 |         selected: list[GraphNode] = []
   300 |         seen_packages: set[str] = set()
   301 |         for node in ranked:
   302 |             top_package = node.qualified_name.split(".")[0]
   303 |             if top_package in seen_packages and len(selected) < 2:
   304 |                 continue
   305 |             selected.append(node)
